2. Facts of the case in writ petition No. 85 of 1974 are that the respondent No. 1 purchased the land from respondent No. 3 with an agreement to reconvey the said land. The agreement is dated 26.4.63 which stipulated that the land will be reconvened if the money is repaid within 10 years. The respondent No. 3 made an application under section 9(4) and (5) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to the Respondent No. 2 for restoration of possession of the said land. This petition was allowed on 30-3-73 and thereafter the respondent No. 1 filed the writ petition urging inter alia that the said order is without lawful authority inasmuch as section 95A of the aforesaid Act does not cover the case of the pure sale with an agreement to recovery. An out and out sale accompanied by an agreement for reconveyance is within the purview of the President's Order Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 whereby provisions of section 95 of the Act have been amended and a new section being section 95A has been inserted in the said Act. A number of writ petitions were filed and the High Court Division disposed of these petitions by one judgment as the same question of law of public importance had been rayed and on consideration of which a certificate was also granted. Vires of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 was also challenged whereby section 95A was inserted and the constitutionality of President's Order No. 24 of 1973 was also challenged. The High Court Division after hearing the arguments came to the conclusion that (a) a transaction of out and out sale; with an agreement to reconvey within the meaning of section 95A must be in sense a mortgage: (b) a transaction of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey is not a transaction within the am bit of section 95A; (c) section 95A has no application to a transaction which has been passed and closed before the relevant President's Order was promulgated (d) section 95A cannot be invoked in respect of a transaction which has been entered into before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation in the area in which the land in question lies. Bangladesh is the appellant. The learned Attorney General appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court Division erred in holding that the word transfer" in section 95 of the East Bengal State Acquisition & Tenancy Act must be construed as meaning a transfer by mortgage. It is contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division committed substantial error of law in adding words into the Statutes. It was canvassed that the intention of the legislature was to cover even sale with an agreement to reconvey and the High Court Division was wrong in applying the different rules of Interpretation to construe the work transfer as transfer by mortgage. It was further contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were wrong in applying the so-called mischief rule as enunciated in Heydorm’s case to hold that the words out and out sale with agreement to reconvey refer to a Mortgage by conditional sale. It was overlooked that a sale with an agreement for reconveyance is distinct from mortgage by conditional sale. The High Court Division had erred in holding that the President's Order 24 of 1973 has led to the constitutional difficulty which, however, was a mere amendment of a grammatical error, Lastly it was contended that the High Court Division had erroneously taken the view that President's Order No. 24 of 1973 affected certain vested right to .property which is vocative of the fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. 

 95A. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, any transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof, either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete unfructuary mortgage for period not exceeding seven years and the provisions of section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Second Amendment) Order 1972". 

 The learned Attorney General has placed the Judgment of the High Court Division which certainly cannot be assailed for brevity. The learned Judges had taken pains to consider the rules of interpretation which would be applicable for interpreting the relevant sections. Considerable attention was devoted as to which of the rules of interpretation should be applied, namely whether the literal rule or golden rule as propounded by Lord Wendeydal or Heydon's rule or mischief rule as suggested by Lord Coke. The High Court Division considered that the effect of impugned law in its literal interpretation is virtually a prohibition against the common form of transaction which is invoked in the society and further this legislation may well be considered discriminatory. It considered that the vested right to a property cannot be extinguished as purported to have been done President's Order No. 24 of 1973 and speculated that the consequences flowing from the impugned Presidential Orders construed literally would amount to a virtual embargo upon this common form of transaction and "if is more than likely that such a form of transaction shall fall into disuse in no time". It considered that the right of repurchase is a privileges granted (or the benefit of the seller which is essentially personal in character. The Pesiderit's Orders were considered in the background of previous law, namely, section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act and disposed of the point by noting that "it is not necessary to speculate whether in view of this prohibition against creating a complete unfructuary mortgage in favour of a person other than a bonafide cultivator, some of the beneficial measures for giving relief to indebted agricultural tenants which were incorporated in the amended section 26G were not considered to be necessary to be included in section 95 at the time when the East Pakistan State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was enacted or where the legislature lost right of those judicial authorities which gave strict interpretation to the unfructuary mortgage as used in section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act in accordance with the terms of section 95(a) of the transfer of Property Act". The High Court Division on such consideration made the rules absolute and set aside the orders passed under section 95 read with section 95A. 

 4. The Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 is a law relating to the landlord and the tenant. East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was promulgated for the acquisition by the State of the interest of the rent-receivers and certain other interest in land and "to define the law relating to tenancies to be held under the State after such a acquisition and other matters connected herewith". Part- V of the Act mainly deals with the rights and obligations of agricultural tenants which was so long controlled and regulated under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act and came in to force in different areas at different points of time, the earliest being 5-8-54 in the Subdivision of Patuakhali and the last being 5-8 65 in the District of Faridpur. 

 5. Section 26G was introduced by amending Act IV of 1982 which came into force on 22-2-29. The object of the legislature was to protect a raiyat "so that no mahajan can keep a raiyat out of his land for more than 15 years at the most" in return for a, petty loan. This section permitted an occupancy raiyat to create a complete unfructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 15 years and did not allow him to create any unfructuary mortgage as defined in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act but the amending Act Of the Bengal Tenancy Act introduced a new definition of "complete unfructuary mortgage" by section 3(3), which says complete unfructuary mortgage means of transfer by a tenant of the right of possession in any land for the advanced or to be advanced by way of loan upon the condition that the loan with all interests thereon shall be deemed to be extinguished by the profit arising from the land during the period of mortgage". Under this sub-section the gradual process of reduction may not follow the strict rules of arithmetic. In other words no question of accounting arises unless an earlier redemption is proposed as contemplated by section 26G(2). It envisages automatic extinction of the loan both principal and interest within the stipulated period no matter whether the profits of land taken by the mortgagee had been of sufficient value to cover the total amount of the loan with interest thereon. The legal effect of it is that after expiry of the stipulated period the property automatically comes back to the mortgagor and the maximum period allowed by law was 15 years. The effect is that no unfructuary mortgage of the raiyati holding when even created can endure for a longer period than 15 years and they will be statutorily redeemed. Registration of documents creating a complete unfructuary mortgage for exceeding 15 years or unfructuary mortgage other than complete unfructuary mortgage was also forbidden and such documents were declared inadmissible in evidence., Thus a drastic change was made by Act IV of 1928 and a new type of mortgage being "complete unfructuary mortgage" was brought as a concept for the benefit of the raiyat. Litigations cropped up as to the retrospectively of his amendment and by Act IV of 1928, the legislature introduced section 26G(1) (a) and declared that every unfructuary mortgage created before 22-2-29 and which was subsisting on or after 1-8-38 (date of the commencement of the amendment) was to be deemed to be a complete unfructuary mortgage for period mentioned in the instrument or 15 years whichever is Jess. Sub-sections (5) and (6) were also inserted by Act VI of 1938 whereby it was provided that after the expiry of the period mentioned in the instrument or 15 years from the date of registration of the compete unfructuary mortgage or from the date of mortgagee’s entering into possession, as the case may be whichever is earlier, a complete unfructuary mortgage or an unfructuary mortgage sha1l be deemed to have been extinguished and the mortgagor there after would on application made either to civil court or revenue court be restored to possession. The Calcutta High Court in a number of decisions held that anomalous mortgage with possession given to the mortgagee, namely mortgage by conditional sale when the mortgagee had entered into possession was not covered by sub-section r) (a) and (5) [Badsha Mia Vs. Mobarrak Ali. 50 C. W.N. 578). Thereafter by amending Act XVIII of 1940 obviously for nullifying those decisions section 260 was further amended which provides that every form of mortgage executed before 22.2.29 and subsisting on or after 1.8.37 was to be deemed complete unfructuary mortgage if possession had been delivered to the mortgagee including a mortgage by conditional sale." The sub-section thus included a1l mortgages executed before 22.2.29 whether unfructuary or "anomalous" provided they were subsisting on 1-8-37 and as regards mortgages executed after the Act of 1928 it came to embrace all such mortgages whether "complete" unfructuary mortgage or "anomalous" mortgage provided they were executed before the Act 1940 and subsisting after the commencement of that Act. Sub-section (4) which created a bar against registration of documents creating unfructuary mortgage for more than 15 years or unfructuary mortgage other than complete unfructuary mortgage now added the "anomalous mortgage" to the list. Thus it is apparent by the amending Acts of 1928 and 1940 the legislature relieved the raiyat from all sorts of mortgages, namely (a) unfructuary mortgage. (b)a mortgage by conditional sale and (C) anomalous mortgages which are known concepts of the Transfer of Property Act. The raiyat can only create a complete unfructuary mortgage for which the definition was supplied by the Amending Act IV of 1928. It is not necessary to consider the incidents of unfructuary mortgage and mortgage by conditional sale or anomalous mortgage which are mentioned in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act. The law extricated the raiyat from those mortgages and laid down that he can only create a complete unfructuary mortgage which is to be valid for a period not exceeding 15 years after which such mortgage is extinguished and on application before the Civil Court or revenue court his possession is restored. Then came East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (E.B. Act XXVIII of 1951). All the rent receiving interest were acquired with effect from 14-4-56 Section 95 of the Act provided that a raiyat could not enter into any form of unfructuary mortgage other than the complete unfructuary mortgage and every such complete unfructuary mortgage is subject to the limitation of section 90. Section 2(b) defined complete unfructuary mortgage which means a transfer by a tenant of the right of possession in any land for the purpose of securing the payment of money on the return of grain advanced or to be advanced by way of loan upon the condition that the loan with all interest thereon, shall be deemed to be extinguished by the profits ensuing from the land during the period of the mortgage". 

 Originally it provided that the period would not exceed 15 years and the registration of documents was made compulsory. It further provided that if it is not a complete usufructuary mortgage or if the documents are not registered then the usufructuary mortgage is void. By the East Pakistan Ordinance XXI of 1969 the period was reduced to 7 years. Thus, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act placed an embargo that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force a raiyat shall not enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than complete usufructuary mortgage." The Transfer of Property Act so far as mortgage of a raiyat holding is concerned is thus displaced Sub-sections (4) and (5) provided for less expensive and less time consuming remedy of redemption and /or restoration of possession by means of application before the authorised officer who will pass the order of restoring possession and, if necessary, by evicting the mortgagee by use of force. The amendment was made by President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and section 95A was inserted by the same President's Order. Section 95A provides that in any transaction when the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct of such holding, etc. for a specified period in lieu of such consideration then such transfer shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for not exceeding 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) will apply for restoration of possession. Thus, the historical background of this legislation is obvious, namely, that the raiyat is to be rescued from the clutches of the money lenders or mohajans who taking advantage of the property of the raiyat would force him to enter into a disadvantageous deal. To protect a raiyat from such transactions, the law-makers came to his rescue prohibiting him from entering into any kind of mortgage other than complete usufructuary mortgage and the maximum period for which he could transfer his land was reduced to 7 years whereupon the debt including the principal and interest stands liquidated and on an application before the authorised officer the raiyat could be put back into possession. Human ingenuity devised new contrivances and the hairsplitting decisions given by various courts as to whether the instrument in question created mortgage by conditional sale or usufructuary mortgage or anomalous mortgage led the legislature to come again to the rescue by disowning all sorts of mortgage other than the "complete usufructuary mortgage." The question as to what about a transaction of an out and out sale with an agreement to recovery has led to numerous litigations and on 4-11-72 President's Order No. 136 of 197). was enacted and section 95A was amended by insertion of the clause : 

 6. The High Court Division missed the real intent of the legislation which originated since 1928, although it seems that it was in the view of the learned Judges, because they themselves considered the laws as "beneficial legislations" but the learned Judges wondered why in enacting section 95 the provisions of section 26G were not kept in view by the legislature. The answer is simple, that by the operation of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act no complete usufructuary mortgage by a raiyat would subsist beyond 15 years, that is why when the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in 1966 all such mortgages were extinguished by operation of law. The legislature, in section 95; provided that the raiyat shall not enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than the complete usufructuary mortgage and to give the complete shape to the social thinking the legislature also prohibited a contract of out and out sale with reconveyance and by a deeming clause had made such transaction as complete usufructuary mortgage. In other words in Bangladesh a raiyat cannot enter into any other transaction of his raiyat-holding except a complete usufructuary mortgage. Thus the process that was started in 1928 found its full expression by the amendment caused by President's Order No. 24 of 1973. The view of the High Court Division that such transactions are an embargo upon the common form of transaction is unwarranted. It is for the legislature to decide that question whether the raiyati's interest will be best protected by creating such embargo. The High Court Division was wrong in saying "that consequences flowing from the President's Order construed literally in undoubtedly absurd and unjust in the context of prevailing legal norms". It is neither absurd not unjust because the vast majority of our people are illiterate agriculturists living in abject poverty and the legislature passed the law to protect their interest in order to save them from the clutches of the money lenders or mohajans from reaping benefits out of their unconscionable bargains. The High Court Division considered that the word "transfer" used in section 95A must be given a restrictive connotation. It means only a transfer in the nature of a mortgage with respect, this kind of construction has been considered as "new terror" in the construction of statute. It would be a new terror in the construction of Acts of Parliament if we were required to limit a word to an unnatural sense because in the same Act which is 'not incorporated or, referred to such interpretation is given to it for the purposes of that Act alone" per Lord Lovedura, LC in Macbeth vs Chistell, 1910 (AC) 220 (223). Lord Mac-Naghten observed in the same case : 

 The anxiety of the High Court Division for interpreting the presidential orders is perceptible when it devoted considerable attention as to whether the Haydon's rule or mischief rule propounded by Lord Coke or Golden Rule of Lord Wendaydal or the learned Judges to devote their attention for the Canons of construction and interpretation when they themselves have found the "broad unanimity" is "to take the whole statute together and construe the said proviso as a part of the said statute." The learned Judge addressed themselves we shall have to interpret the words literally at the first instance by applying the literal rule, but if we find that as a result of such literal interpretation certain consequences do arise which are absurd or unjust, it would set the court to inquire if it was the intention of the law-maker to use the words in their ordinary significance. Having propounded the principle correctly, the learned Judges took pains to find that the amendment by President's Order No. 24 of 1973 in inserting the word "or" the legislature created a new legislation. If section 1959 is perused then it will be evident that the word "or" has been inserted for grammatical reasons because the expression "either" is to be associated with the expression "or". When President's Order No. 136 of 1972 inserted the expression "either" by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey the expression or was a mere grammatical requirement which as has been contended by the learned Attorney-General is that in the absence of any amendment such expression could have been supplied by the Court as cause omisus. Even Lord Wensbydale who pro pounded the golden rule of construction stated: 

 7. Mr SR Pal, Amicus Curiae has rightly pointed out that the High Court Division missed the deeming provision in section 95A which categorically says "shall notwithstanding anything contained in the documents relating to the transfer be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage". Since 1928 recourse was taken of the deeming provision by the legislature and all sorts of mortgage, usufructuary mortgage, mortgages by conditional sale, anomalous have been displaced by providing that all such mortgages by a raiyat shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage" for which a definition was given in the Bengal Tenancy Act. The learned Judges then considered that the literal construction of the President's Orders would entail "constitutional difficulties". The learned Attorney-General has pointed out that the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a protected legislation with all the amendments. Exception has been taken by the High Court Division to this argument and it is said it cannot be accepted unless clear indication has been given in the constitution in this behalf. Article 47 read with the 1st Schedule of the Constitution has protected this law and clear indication has been given in the Constitution itself and when the parent legislation is immune from attack the consequential amendments are to be viewed in that light, namely, for giving effect to the parent legislation unless it would be shown that the amendment minus the protection, is otherwise unconstitutional. No such case has been or could be made out in any of these appeals and no argument was advanced on behalf of the respondent. 

 9. Mr Shamsul Huq Chowdhury appearing for the respondents could not show as to how discrimination has been made when the legislation was passed to save a class of people for whom even the learned Judges have found a rational basis. As for the violation of fundamental right, the right to property is given in Article 42 of the Constitution but subject to reasonable restriction. Clause (2) of Article 42 has no relevancy because that operates in a different context, namely, compulsory acquisition, nationalisation or requisition. The High Court Division has fallen into error by construing the expression "transfer" in the context of the Transfer of Property Act which is evident from their own observation "the agreement to recovery shall have to be incorporated in the deed affecting the transfer in view of the provision to section 58 (c) of Transfer of Property Act". Here lies the error because since 1928 the legislature wanted to take out the transaction of the raiyat from the purview of Transfer of Property Act for which specific definition was supplied, namely, "complete usufructuary mortgage" in the Bengal Tenancy Act. 

 11. Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President's Order Nos. 88 and 116 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 are all valid legislation for affecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vices. (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either way of out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of sections 95 (4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question :(4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to recovery, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 : and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed.
